content:
If your home is getting harder to manage because of arthritis and frailty, sheltered or extra care housing may be options to consider.

This guide explains the main types and what to ask. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Sheltered housing

  • Self-contained flats or bungalows for older people.
  • Often a scheme manager or warden, though not always on site.
  • An emergency alarm system.
  • Shared areas such as a lounge or garden.
  • Care is not usually provided, but you can arrange it separately.

Extra care housing

Extra care housing, sometimes called assisted living, offers your own home with care and support staff on site. It may suit people who need regular help but want to keep their own front door.

Questions to ask

  • Is there step-free access and a lift?
  • Are bathrooms accessible, such as level-access showers?
  • What are the rent and service charges?
  • What help is available, and at what times?
  • Can adaptations be made?

How to apply

Apply through your council or housing associations, or look at private schemes. A needs assessment from your council may help if you need care. Age UK and other advice services can explain options.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Is sheltered housing a care home?

No. You live independently in your own home.

Who pays for care in extra care housing?

It depends on your needs and finances. Ask your council about assessment.
